title: They tried to make him famous…
paragraphs:
They tried to make him famous…
but he refused to take the credit.
And that’s what makes this story dangerous.

Because most of us don’t fall when we’re weak.
We fall when we’re seen.

A man who couldn’t walk for years suddenly stands.
Bones strengthen. Ankles lock. Muscles respond.

And in seconds—
the invisible becomes undeniable.

The crowd gasps.
Eyes widen.
Attention shifts.
Not to God.
To Peter.
And here’s the tension—don’t miss this.

This was the perfect moment to build a name.
A following.
A reputation.
One miracle… and you can become someone.
But Peter does something that will confront your soul.
He rejects the spotlight.
Let’s be honest.

We don’t always sin in rebellion.
Sometimes we sin in applause.

You prayed—and it worked.
You spoke—and people listened.
You led—and it succeeded.
And slowly… subtly… silently…
You start believing the power is yours.

Not fully.
Not consciously.
But enough.

Enough to enjoy the credit.
Enough to crave the recognition.
Enough to forget where it came from.
That’s the quiet danger.

Pride doesn’t always roar.
Sometimes it whispers, “You did good.”
But Peter interrupts the illusion.
“Why do you stare at us, as though by our own power or godliness we had made him walk?” (Acts 3:12)
Feel the weight of that.
He refuses to let admiration turn into idolatry.
He refuses to let a miracle become a mirror.
He refuses to let people confuse the vessel with the Source.
And then he redirects everything.
“By faith in the name of Jesus, this man… has been made strong. It is Jesus’ name and the faith that comes through Him that has completely healed him.” (Acts 3:16)

Not my power.
Not my holiness.
Not my reputation.
Jesus.
Always Jesus.
Here’s the deeper truth.
Peter wasn’t always like this.

This is the same man who once said,
“Even if all fall away… I never will.”
Confidence.
Boldness.
Self-assurance.
And then?

He denied Jesus.
Three times.
In one night.
That failure broke something in him.
Or rather—
It broke him open.

Because when you’ve seen your own weakness up close…
you stop pretending you’re strong.

When you’ve failed publicly…
you stop craving public praise.

When grace rescues you from your worst moment…
you stop acting like you deserve your best ones.
Some scholars interpret Peter’s bold humility here as the fruit of deep repentance after his denial. Not perfection—but transformation.
And that’s where many miss it.

Humility is not thinking less of yourself.
It’s seeing yourself accurately before a holy God.

Broken.
Dependent.
Carried by grace.
Let me say something that might sting a little:
If God answered your prayers the way you secretly want credit… would you still point people to Jesus?
Or would you start collecting what belongs to Him?
Because Scripture is clear:
“God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6)
Not ignores.
Opposes.

That means pride doesn’t just slow your walk with God.
It puts you in resistance against Him.
But here’s the beauty of the Gospel.

God doesn’t just expose pride.
He redeems people trapped in it.
Peter is proof.

A man who once boasted in his loyalty
becomes a man who boasts only in Christ.

A man who once failed under pressure
becomes a man who stands under power.
Not because he improved himself.
But because Jesus restored him.
After the resurrection, Jesus didn’t discard Peter.
He pursued him.
“Do you love Me?” (John 21:15–17)
Not: “Why did you fail Me?”
But: “Will you return to Me?”
That’s grace.

Not earned.
Not deserved.
But freely given.
And that’s the invitation for you.
Because maybe your struggle isn’t loud sin.
Maybe it’s quiet pride.

The need to be seen.
The hunger to be affirmed.
The subtle shift from “God did it” to “I did well.”
And you feel it.
That tension.
That internal applause you don’t want to admit.
Listen carefully.

The power flowing through your life is real.
But it was never yours.
“For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you did receive it, why do you boast as though you did not?” (1 Corinthians 4:7)
Everything you carry is borrowed glory.

Every gift is grace.
Every open door is mercy.
Every impact is Jesus moving through you.
So what do we do?
We return it.
We give the glory back.
Not as a performance.
But as surrender.
Right now—pause.
Check your heart.
Where have you been taking credit?
Where have you been enjoying attention more than honoring Christ?
Where have you subtly stepped onto a throne that was never yours?
This is not condemnation.
This is invitation.
Repent.
Not with shame.
But with clarity.
Turn back.
Step down.
Lift Him up.
Because the goal was never for people to see you.
It was always for people to see Jesus.

Crucified for your sin.
Risen for your salvation.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified freely by His grace through the redemption that came by Christ Jesus.” (Romans 3:23–24)
That includes pride.
That includes you.
So come back.

Not polished.
Not pretending.
But honest.
And let your life say:

“The power is real…
but the glory belongs to Jesus.”
Let it be your declaration.
